Engineers are examining a redesign of certain HFIR sub-systems to TIG weld instead of electron beam weld as was previously done. This redesign will require major engineering and quality work. A similar approach could be taken for copper accelerators where the critical welds are electron Page 37 of 55 “Manufacturing full-scale high gradient copper accelerators: Electron beam welding and allied processes” Prepared for the U.S. Department of Energy ARDAP program beam welded (i.e. those that interact with the interior of the cavity) while other welds are completed in a clean room or glove box environment with laser or TIG welding. This would reduce the required number of welds from a EBW job shop. If these welds could be standardized it would also significantly improve the chances of a job shop wanting to take the job. B.3.4 Potential DOE-Science Collaborative Models for EBW Electron beam welding is a critical technology for advanced applications in a broad array of industries including power generation and engineering, semiconductor manufacturing, aerospace, transportation, e- mobility, nuclear, defense, and scientific investigation (e.g. accelerators, fusion reactors, beam lines). All of these sectors are supported by DOE research and as such various labs across the DOE ecosystem require electron beam welding for their applications. Potential collaborators are listed below. Science Focused: The DOE national labs focused on beam line science and accelerator science require electron beam welding for their infrastructure and components. These labs include Brookhaven, Fermilab, Berkeley Lab, Oak Ridge National Lab, Argonne National Lab, Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, and Jefferson Lab. Coordination between these labs on required electron beam welding facilities either by consistent contracting, or a centralized internal facility and agreement with a private contractor may be beneficial. Engineers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Plasma Science and Fusion Center recently completed a significant amount of electron beam welding waveguides made from copper alloy GR-Cop 84[67]. Additional EBW is forecasted, especially for large chamber EBW which can handle extended waveguide runs. Broad Focused Manufacturing: The Oakridge National Lab Manufacturing Demonstration Facility is a unique, 110,000 sq. ft. facility focused on advanced materials and manufacturing. While the internal equipment hosted at this facility rotates according to needs of industry and government, it currently has electron beam welding capabilities and are specifically setup to support research and development of manufacturing for advanced materials. It is unlikely that this capability could transition to full-scale production. Researchers at the Materials Science and Technology Division of ORNL has also recently completed an extremely detailed analysis risks and advantages of thick-section electron beam welding of light water reactor pressure vessels [29]. As part of a 2014 New York State economic development initiative called the Buffalo Billion, EWI was selected to establish an advanced manufacturing center in Buffalo, N.Y called the Buffalo Manufacturing Works. EWI, previously known as Edison Welding Institute, is a nonprofit engineering and technology organization dedicated to developing, testing, and implementing advanced manufacturing technologies for industry.
